transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-21
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Leah Kim, Daniel Ortega (Redwood); Mark Davies (CTO), Aisha Khan (DevOps), Tom Riley (Product), Sara Li (Security)
Recording link: https://app.fireflies.ai/recording/ff-2026-09-21-bridgepoint-8743 (shared)

Summary (auto): quick demo of org/project keys, how rate limits and quotas are applied, and options for per-tenant billing and dedicated capacity.

Transcript:
[00:00] Leah Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I think we have about 40 minutes, we'll go through the rate-limits and org/project keys demo. Daniel's going to drive the console and I'll cover commercial and next steps.
[00:18] Mark Davies: Great, thanks Leah. Quick context — Bridgepoint runs a bunch of internal products, we want to expose LLM features per product line but keep billing and quotas separate, and we have strict compliance requirements.
[00:35] Daniel Ortega: Awesome, Mark. I'll share my screen now, give me a sec. (murmur) Can you see the Redwood Console?
[00:44] Aisha Khan: Yes, I can see it. There's a bit of lag on my end.
[00:48] Daniel Ortega: Cool, so top-level is the org view. You can see overall usage, cost, and per-project breakdown. We're demoing the org/project keys model — org-level key gives blanket access for admins, project keys are scoped to a single project and can have their own quotas and billing tags.
[01:10] Tom Riley: Quick question — if we use project keys for customer-facing apps, can we rotate them independently?
[01:18] Daniel Ortega: Yep, you can rotate per-key. We also support short-lived keys via our API for ephemeral workloads. (small pause) This is important for multi-tenant isolation.
[01:32] Sara Li: How does rate limiting map to billing? We need a way to cap spend per project and also enforce throughput limits.
[01:40] Leah Kim: Good question. You have two levers — quotas and rate limits. Quotas are monthly units (tokens or embedding units) that stop usage when exceeded, and rate limits are QPS or tokens/sec throttles with burst windows. Billing segmentation is done via project tags so invoices can be split by project.
[01:58] Mark Davies: So can we set a hard stop for a project if spend hits X? We don't want runaway costs.
[02:06] Leah Kim: Yes, set a hard quota + notifications. You can also configure soft limits that alert first and hard limits that block requests.
[02:15] Aisha Khan: For our environment we're leaning toward hosted API for dev and dedicated for production. How do quotas behave across hosted vs dedicated?
[02:25] Daniel Ortega: On hosted, quotas are enforced in our control plane and are tenant-aware. For dedicated, you still configure quotas but we can enforce at the pool level plus per-project policing — and we can apply local rate-limiter instances to reduce cross-tenant interference.
[02:41] [02:41] Mark Davies: When you say "dedicated pool" what are the scaling/burst options?
[02:44] Daniel Ortega: We offer reserved capacity with configurable burst capacity. For example, you can commit to baseline GPU capacity and allow X% burst for spiky traffic. There's an autoscaler with policies — we can show the SLA/RPOs after.
[02:57] Tom Riley: And how do we map projects to billing? We have internal projects and customer projects, we want separate invoices per product line.
[03:07] Leah Kim: Each project carries billing tags. You can export a CSV or hook into billing APIs. Many customers use project tags to map to chargeback systems.
[03:15] Daniel Ortega: I'm jumping into the rate limits UI now — under Policies > Rate Limits you create rules by scope: org, project, or key. Rules have a window (per second/minute), a burst allowance, and an enforcement action (throttle, queue, or reject).
[03:33] [03:33] Aisha Khan: Is enforcement consistent across regions? We have traffic across us-west and eu-central.
[03:39] Daniel Ortega: Yes, rules are global by default but you can scope by region. We also have smart routing so if a region is constrained, you can route to another region or fallback to a cheaper model variant.
[03:53] Mark Davies: Security piece — we need KMS integration and audit logs for all key actions.
[03:59] Sara Li: And SOC 2 evidence for data handling, plus some customers require keys to be stored in their KMS.
[04:07] Leah Kim: We support customer-managed KMS for Private deployments, and for Dedicated we have KMS integrations. Audit logs are retained and accessible through the Console and exported to S3 or SIEM. We can add retention length as part of the enterprise agreement.
[04:21] [04:21] Mark Davies: Can you show an example of per-project rate-limits getting hit? We want to see the UX and how graceful degradation looks.
[04:28] Daniel Ortega: Sure — I'll simulate a burst on project 'mobile-app'. (typing) Ok, I bumped a load generator. On the dashboard you can see request rate spike, and the project-level limiter starts queuing requests once we hit the burst threshold.
[04:42] Tom Riley: Looks like requests are queued — what's the latency impact?
[04:46] Daniel Ortega: Depends on policy — you can choose queue length and timeout. For low-latency routes we recommend a conservative burst and fallback to a smaller model. For non-critical async workloads you can allow deeper queues.
[04:59] Aisha Khan: Is the fallback automatic to a smaller model or do we need to configure it?
[05:04] Daniel Ortega: You can configure automatic fallback policies — route by latency, cost, or region. Fallback can be to a quantized model variant or a lower tier.
[05:13] [05:13] Mark Davies: What about meters — we want near-real-time visibility for cost.
[05:17] Leah Kim: Console gives per-minute and per-route token metrics, and you can stream logs into your metrics pipeline. There's also token-level cost attribution so you can see spend per project per model.
[05:27] Sara Li: For compliance we need an immutable audit of key rotations and access.
[05:31] Daniel Ortega: We keep an immutable activity log for key lifecycle events and admin actions. Those logs are exportable. One caveat — in hosted mode we manage the control plane, but all key use events are included in the audit trail. For Private we can route logs directly into your SIEM.
[05:47] [05:47] Tom Riley: Any limitations on number of projects or keys? We're planning ~50 internal projects and 200 external client projects at scale.
[05:55] Daniel Ortega: The platform supports thousands of projects and keys; at that scale we usually recommend a structure with orgs -> projects -> keys and possibly sub-project tags for billing. We can show best practices in the implementation guide.
[06:09] Mark Davies: If a project is blocked due to quota, can we auto-notify slack or create a ticket?
[06:16] Leah Kim: Yes, you can hook quota events to notifications — Slack, PagerDuty, Webhooks, or auto-creating issues in your ticketing system.
[06:25] [06:25] Aisha Khan: Let's talk about API usage — what's the header or param for project key vs org key? We want an easy dev experience.
[06:32] Daniel Ortega: You pass the API key in the Authorization header as usual. Project keys are scoped and carry metadata; the control plane maps that key to project context. We also have SDK helpers to configure per-project clients.
[06:45] Tom Riley: What about rate-limits enforced at the gateway vs at runtime? Any consistency issues?
[06:51] Daniel Ortega: We enforce both — an edge gateway layer for quick rejects and runtime limiters for more nuanced queueing and KV-cache-safe operations. There's eventual consistency in metrics but enforcement is deterministic per request. Sometimes the transcriptions... words get swapped but enforcement is still deterministic.
[07:12] [07:12] Mark Davies: Regarding billing — do you do invoice per org or can we get per-project invoices?
[07:18] Leah Kim: We can produce granular billing exports and per-project allocation. For enterprise customers we often provide a billing API to pull per-project chargebacks.
[07:27] Sara Li: On the topic of security reviews — we will need the security pack and SOC2 docs. Also we might ask for a penetration test checklist.
[07:36] Leah Kim: Absolutely — I'll include our security pack and arrange a follow-up with the Redwood security team for a deeper session.
[07:42] [07:42] Daniel Ortega: Back on the console — I'll open an example policy. Here's a rate limit rule: scope=project:mobile-app, window=1s, limit=10 requests, burst=20. Action=queue, queue_timeout=500ms. You can also attach labels and apply to API routes/endpoints.
[07:58] Aisha Khan: Could we apply a per-customer quota for embeddings differently from generation tokens?
[08:04] Daniel Ortega: Yes, quotas are resource-type aware — you can set separate quotas for embeddings units, token-gen, and fine-tune jobs.
[08:13] Mark Davies: Does the KV cache affect billing? If we cache prefixes does it reduce tokens charged?
[08:18] Daniel Ortega: Caching reduces compute and typically reduces token usage because shared prefixes won't be reprocessed; billing is based on tokens processed, so effective caching generally lowers costs. There are caveats around privacy for shared caches — for multi-tenant we isolate caches unless you explicitly enable cross-project caching.
[08:36] [08:36] Tom Riley: What about rate limiting for function calls / tool calling? Is that separate?
[08:41] Daniel Ortega: We expose multi-dimensional rate limits; you can limit on request count, token throughput, or semantic actions like function/tool calls.
[08:51] Leah Kim: I want to highlight the Optimize suggestions — the product will recommend batching configs and quantization profiles based on observed workload, which can reduce cost per token. So for a given project's traffic pattern we can suggest a more aggressive quantization and a batching window.
[09:05] Aisha Khan: Do those recommendations change over time?
[09:08] Daniel Ortega: Yes, Optimize is continuous — it watches latency/throughput and will surface suggestions; you opt-in to apply them.
[09:15] [09:15] Mark Davies: Any notable gotchas for HIPAA-like customers? Possibly PII leakage in logs?
[09:21] Sara Li: We need to validate data flows.
[09:24] Leah Kim: For HIPAA customers we recommend Private or Dedicated with VPC and controlled logging. You can disable transcript logging and restrict what is persisted. We also support data redaction hooks.
[09:36] Daniel Ortega: Also, for on-prem or air-gapped options, keys and KMS can be fully customer-managed, and logs stay within your environment.
[09:45] [09:45] Tom Riley: Can you demo setting a project quota now? We want to see the UX.
[09:50] Daniel Ortega: Sure, under Projects > mobile-app > Quotas. Create quota: limit=100k tokens/month, action=hard-stop, notify=email+webhook. Saving... OK it's applied. You can see the enforcement metric.
[10:06] Mark Davies: If we set a hard-stop and then need an emergency override, who can do that?
[10:12] Leah Kim: Admins in the org can temporarily bump quotas or apply an override key. We also support a delegated billing role if you'd rather have finance handle it.
[10:22] [10:22] Aisha Khan: How will this integrate with our CI? We want deploys to create ephemeral keys for tests and rotate them automatically.
[10:29] Daniel Ortega: We have an API to mint ephemeral keys with TTL and restrict scope. Many customers integrate that into CI.
[10:36] Mark Davies: SLA question — if a project is throttled due to noisy neighbor on shared hosted tier, what's the guarantee?
[10:43] Leah Kim: On hosted we have fairness and isolation heuristics but for strict guarantees we recommend Dedicated where we can assure throughput per pool and offer SLA-backed percentiles.
[10:53] [10:53] Tom Riley: Can we get an export of current rate-limits and project mappings as JSON?
[10:57] Daniel Ortega: Yes, you can export via API or download from Console. I'll attach a sample JSON in the follow-up.
[11:06] [11:06] Mark Davies: One more on quotas — is there an API to check quota remaining programmatically?
[11:11] Daniel Ortega: Yes, there's a /quota endpoint that returns remaining units per project/key and projected burn rate.
[11:18] Leah Kim: Ok, quick recap of what we showed: org vs project keys, per-project quotas and rate limits, enforcement actions (queue/throttle/reject), billing segmentation, KMS/audit options, and Optimize suggestions.
[11:29] [11:29] Mark Davies: That was super helpful. Next step for us is to scope a pilot: 3 projects (mobile-app, web-portal, analytics), expected baseline QPS ~120, peak ~900. We want cost estimate and a security review.
[11:42] Leah Kim: Great — action items: Leah will send pricing and dedicated estimator; Daniel will share sample configs and export; Mark will confirm pilot scope and schedule security follow-up.
[11:54] Aisha Khan: One micro ask — can we get an example of the Slack webhook payload when quota is hit?
[11:59] Daniel Ortega: Yup, I'll include a sample in the follow-up.
[12:04] [12:04] Sara Li: Also please include SOC2 cert and pen-test checklist.
[12:07] Leah Kim: Will do. Thanks all. We'll follow up by end of this week.
[12:13] [12:13] Meeting end: 15:42 PDT
